meta.method: Audio fingerprint segments for original-dialogue regions; narration read by OCR of viral caption band (tesseract, 4 fps); narration-region source times established by side-by-side frame comparison against source proxy (burned SOURCE band) at 1 s steps. AutoStory from story-spine.json + resolved-timeline + old_align_segments + transcript.
notes: Viral 15.0-46.5 is one continuous source run 13.8-45.3 (offset -1.2) with narration over the first 18.5 s; 46.5-78.0 is one continuous run 51.2-82.7 (offset +4.7) with narration over the first 16.5 s.
Viral 78.0-94.5 source mapping is approximate (visual, +/-1.5 s; one micro-cut likely near 94.5).
AutoStory contains no narration (voice status not_applicable on all 16 segments).

viralStoryScope: One incident, one continuous window: the 911-call arrival through the discovery of the restrained daughter and the first competing claims (source 13.8-121.0 covers ~88% of runtime), plus two short narrated forward bridges (379.5-386.3, 431.8-439.6) that exist only to move to the interrogation and set the cliffhanger. Packaged explicitly as Part 1.
autoStoryStoryScope: Declared episode 8.5-1415.7 s (~82% of the source). Content drawn from four separate phases: entry (8.5-58.5), mother interview at three disjoint moments (223.8, 431.6-439.6, 749.4), and the boyfriend's outdoor interview ~20 min later (1327.7-1415.7). No narration bridges; 5 jumps of 177-576 s.
viralCentralViewerQuestion: The parents were reported as attacking their daughter but claim they're the ones handling a disturbed child - who is the real aggressor, and will the mother's own explanation get her arrested?
autoStoryCentralViewerQuestion: (EDL) 'What really happened between the daughter and her parents, and who is telling the truth?' - in the cut, the question drifts from the restraint, to the mother's partial admission, to a third party's retrospective account, and never converges on a concrete expected outcome.

viralScopeBoundary.narrative: Starts at the officer's approach (after the source's own intro text) and stops at the moment testimony begins: the mother starts explaining what happened. Everything after ~121 s is excluded except two narrated bridge shots; the admission itself, the daughter's and boyfriend's accounts, and the arrest are all held back. The boundary is placed exactly where the conflict changes mode from physical (restraint) to verbal (interrogation), leaving the resolution for Part 2.

autoStoryScopeBoundary.narrative: No clear boundary: the cut leaves the physical incident at 46.5 s of source (output 26 s) and samples interviews across ~20 minutes, stopping mid-interview before the arrest decision (1483-1712). It includes secondary storylines (boyfriend's retrospective account) while excluding the actual resolution, so it is neither a complete story nor a focused Part 1.

answers.whyExcludedLaterEvents: The later ~27 minutes are mostly static interviews that re-describe the same fight from different speakers (mother 222-830, daughter 845-1200, boyfriend 1206-1411), plus procedure (civil-property talk, paperwork). They add perspectives, not new on-screen events. The human kept the one on-camera confrontation and translated the necessary gist of the later testimony (mental-health claim, 'just wanted to leave') into two narrated sentences over continuous restraint footage (78-94.5). The arrest (1604-1712) is excluded deliberately as the Part 2 payoff the ending promises.
answers.whyOneStory: All 117.6 s serve one arc - allegation -> discovery -> competing claims -> accuser becomes suspect - inside one location and ~2 minutes of real time. Every speaker is someone the viewer has already seen in the bathroom. Nothing requires introducing a new place or a new witness.
answers.whereIsBoundary: Source 121 s (dense coverage end) narratively; the physical confrontation ends and questioning begins. Bridge/tease shots at 379.5-386.3 and 431.8-439.6 are used only as picture under narration pointing past the boundary.
answers.activeViewerQuestion: 0-15: what is happening upstairs? 15-46: why are parents accused, and why does the mother seem to be asking for help? 46-63: pays off (man pinning daughter). 63-94: whose version is true (runaway/mental episode vs adult trying to leave)? 94-117: will the mother's own explanation incriminate her -> arrest?
answers.whatChangesBeatToBeat: Each beat either adds a new fact about the same confrontation (allegation, identity, claim, counter-claim) or pays off a withheld visual. Location/time changes only when a narrated sentence carries the viewer across them (103.0 'as officers finally get the stepfather to release...').
answers.lossIfSecondaryBeatRemoved: Removing 26.5-33.5 (quiet-home approach) costs only contrast and pacing. Removing 94.5-103 (mother's 'family discussion about boundaries and rules') weakens the ending: 'her own words' then refers to words the viewer never heard. Removing 103-109.8 leaves an unexplained jump from restraint to interview.
answers.coldOpenStructure: 0-15 = source 38.8-53.8, original audio: plea at the door and the stair climb, cut to black just before the bathroom is visible. It is an in-incident flash-forward only ~25 s of source ahead of the rewind point, and it withholds the key visual (the pinned daughter) rather than showing it.
answers.rewindBehavior: 15.0 hard rewind to source 13.8 (arrival) with narration giving the allegation; plays forward continuously, re-shows 38.8-45.3 in context with original audio (now meaningful: the 'help her' comes from an accused parent), then skips the already-seen stair climb (45.3-51.2) and goes straight to the withheld reveal at 51.2. The replay is short, contextualized and non-redundant.
answers.endingFunction: Narrated cliffhanger (109.8-117.6) over the mother starting her explanation: names a specific expected payoff (her own words -> arrest) and stops before delivering it; 'Part 1' frames the missing resolution as a promise, not an omission.
answers.narrationRole: ~66 s of 117.6. Uses: (1) exposition the footage can't show (the call, the allegation), (2) identity labelling, (3) compressing claims made much later in the source into single sentences without cutting away from the incident, (4) time compression (4+ min into one sentence), (5) the cliffhanger. Narration always runs over footage that is causally continuous with the dialogue beats around it.
answers.dialogueRole: ~51.5 s. Original audio is reserved for moments where the words are the conflict and understandable without context: the plea at the door, the pinned daughter's 'please help me/it's hurting', the direct mother-vs-daughter clash, and the mother's controlling 'rules of the house' framing. No talking-head retrospective interviews are used as dialogue.

genericEditorialPrinciples.principle: Pick one causally continuous incident window and let it carry most of the runtime; treat everything outside it as material to summarize, not to cut to.
genericEditorialPrinciples.evidenceFromViral: ~88% of output from source 13.8-121.0; only 14.6 s from outside it, both used as narrated picture (103-117.6).
genericEditorialPrinciples.failureInAutoStory: Five jumps of 177-576 s across 8.5-1415.7; 28 s (42%) from a separate outdoor interview 20 minutes later (output 39-67).
genericEditorialPrinciples.generalization: Score candidate windows by causal continuity and on-screen action density; cap the share of runtime taken from outside the chosen window and require any out-of-window cut to be a deliberate bridge or tease.

genericEditorialPrinciples.principle: Use narration to compress exposition, identity, off-screen claims and elapsed time, so the picture can stay on the incident.
genericEditorialPrinciples.evidenceFromViral: 78-94.5 condenses the parents' mental-health claim and the daughter's 'I just wanted to leave' version (from much later testimony) over continuous restraint footage; 103-109.8 compresses ~4 minutes into one sentence.
genericEditorialPrinciples.failureInAutoStory: No narration at all; it tries to convey the same claims with literal source fragments (2 s at 749.4, 4 s at 223.8) that don't contain the information the EDL says they do, and jumps with no bridge.
genericEditorialPrinciples.generalization: When information lives far from the chosen window, or is buried in long testimony, narrate it; reserve cutaways for information that only the picture can deliver.

genericEditorialPrinciples.principle: The cold open should withhold the key reveal, come from the same incident a little way ahead, and the rewind should replay it in context without redundancy.
genericEditorialPrinciples.evidenceFromViral: 0-15 ends right before the bathroom is visible; the rewind goes back only ~25 s of source; on replay, the stair climb already seen is skipped (45.3-51.2) and the reveal is paid off at 46.5-63.
genericEditorialPrinciples.failureInAutoStory: The hook shows the reveal outright (output 4-6, 'get this off of me'), so the rewind (6-26) replays context the viewer no longer needs, and then the story leaves the incident.
genericEditorialPrinciples.generalization: Choose a hook that asks a question (sound, motion toward danger), cut before the answer, and on the return pass cut out what was already seen and go straight to the payoff.

genericEditorialPrinciples.principle: Every beat must change the viewer's state on the same central question, and the cut must actually contain the line that does it.
genericEditorialPrinciples.evidenceFromViral: Beat sequence allegation (15) -> counter-frame (33.5) -> visual confirmation (46.5) -> victim voice (63) -> direct clash (70) -> both claims named (78-94.5) -> antagonist's own framing (94.5) -> setup of self-incrimination (109.8).
genericEditorialPrinciples.failureInAutoStory: beat_008 claims 'lashing out' but carries a text-message detail; beat_010 stops before 'hair pulling and slapping'; beat_011 is a content-free 2 s fragment; beats 013/015 repeat things already shown or known.
genericEditorialPrinciples.generalization: Verify each beat's claimed information against its transcript span before accepting it; drop beats whose delta is zero or duplicates an earlier beat or visual.

genericEditorialPrinciples.principle: End on a specific, forward-pointing consequence taken from inside the scope, and leave the resolution out rather than half in.
genericEditorialPrinciples.evidenceFromViral: 109.8-117.6: 'her own words might just provide the exact evidence the police need to make an arrest' over the mother beginning to talk; the arrest (1604-1712) is withheld for Part 2.
genericEditorialPrinciples.failureInAutoStory: Ends at 1410.7-1415.7 with the boyfriend's closing words and the officer turning to a new question; no stated expected outcome, while the true payoff (arrest) is also missing.
genericEditorialPrinciples.generalization: Choose the boundary where the conflict changes mode; close with the concrete question the next segment would answer, and either include a payoff completely or promise it explicitly.

genericEditorialPrinciples.principle: Use original dialogue for self-explanatory confrontation; don't use retrospective talking heads as primary story beats.
genericEditorialPrinciples.evidenceFromViral: All 51.5 s of original audio is in-the-moment conflict (plea, pain, clash, mother's framing); later interviews appear only as narrated gist.
genericEditorialPrinciples.failureInAutoStory: Output 26-67 (61%) is retrospective interview audio, mostly static shots, re-describing violence the viewer saw in the first 6 s.
genericEditorialPrinciples.generalization: Rank dialogue spans by whether they show the conflict happening versus describing it later; prefer the former and narrate the latter.
